title: Ice and Snow Jobsite Safety: Rules Our Crews Live By
desc: The ice and snow safety rules our framing crews follow all winter — deck clearing, ladder discipline, cold-weather PPE, and when we call a weather day.
body:
We're framing through another Upper Midwest winter right now, and this stretch — late December through February — is when jobsites hurt people if the rules go soft. After a lot of winters framing multi-family and commercial projects across Minnesota, North Dakota, Wisconsin, and Montana, our crews run on a short list of non-negotiables. Here they are.

The deck gets cleared before anything else happens

First hour of every morning after snow: shovels and ice melt, not nail guns. Nobody walks plates, sets walls, or rolls trusses on a deck with snow or frost on it. And we never sheath over snow — moisture trapped under sheathing is a callback waiting to happen, and a snow-covered subfloor hides every hole and every cord. Clearing costs us thirty to sixty minutes of production. It's the cheapest insurance we buy all day.

Access is treated like a work area, not an afterthought

  • Every ladder, stair, and ramp gets cleared and gritted before the first climb, and re-checked after breaks — refreeze is sneakier than the first ice.
  • Three points of contact on ladders, period. Tools go up on a rope, not in a hand.
  • Walk paths around the building get maintained all day. Most winter injuries aren't falls from height — they're ankles and wrists at ground level.

Fall protection tightens up, it doesn't loosen

Slick surfaces shrink the margin for error, so winter is when we're strictest about anchors and tie-off. Harnesses get fitted over winter layers — a harness adjusted for a T-shirt in July doesn't fit a guy in insulated bibs — and we check that lanyards and retractables move freely, because they can behave differently in hard cold.

Cold management is production management

A cold framer is a slow, careless framer. Our rules of thumb: layered clothing with a wind-blocking shell, insulated gloves that still let you handle a nailer, and warm-up rotations that get more frequent as the wind chill drops. Foremen watch their crews for the early signs of trouble — clumsiness, slurred speech, the guy who's stopped complaining about the cold. That last one sounds like a joke; it isn't.

Wind rules the crane

Truss and wall picks get planned around the forecast, not squeezed in despite it. Wind limits that feel conservative in July are firm in January, because gusts plus ice plus numb hands is exactly how a tag line gets away from somebody. When it's blowing, we build product on the deck and save the picks for the calm window.

Housekeeping in the cold

Cords and air hoses stiffen and coil in the cold and turn into trip hazards fast. We keep them routed, keep compressors drained so frozen condensate doesn't kill them, and keep heaters — where we use them — away from anything they can cook. A tidy winter site isn't about looking good for the owner's drive-by; it's about not falling down.

When we call a weather day

There's no single magic temperature. We look at actual wind chill, what the crew is doing that day (deck work in open wind is different than first-floor walls in shelter), visibility, and whether ice is actively falling. When the honest answer is that guys will spend more energy staying safe than building, we call it. A lost day costs a few line items on the schedule; an injury costs a man his winter and the project far more. Our multi-family framing schedule guide covers how we build weather days into winter durations so nobody is surprised.

GCs sometimes ask whether all this slows us down. It does the opposite — crews that trust the site keep producing all winter, which is exactly why year-round framing works in this climate. The full scope of what our crews handle is on our services page.

Framing a project this winter or planning one for spring? Reach out — we'll bring the crew that knows how to work in this weather.
